newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Socialists mull provisional rule in Belgrade - sources.
newsitem.headline: Socialists mull provisional rule in Belgrade - sources.

text.p: Serbia's ruling Socialists might try to defuse popular protests over annulled local elections by imposing provisional municipal rule in Belgrade for two months and then calling a new vote, political sources said on Tuesday.

But the sources, close to President Slobodan Milosevic's secretive inner circle, stressed this was only one of various options proposed in an unresolved internal debate. They conceded it would almost certainly not placate opposition protesters.
Political analysts say the only constant in a confused decision-making process so far has been an effort to stall for time but such tactics might be running out of steam.

Nine consecutive weeks of mass street protests over the nullified municipal elections won by an opposition bloc degenerated into rare violence on Monday night when weary riot police dispensed with restraint and clubbed some demonstrators.

The incidents in Belgrade, coupled with a new outbreak of anti-government bloodshed in the Albanian-majority province of Kosovo, signalled that Milosevic could not afford to drag the election crisis out for much longer, analysts said.

"At a time when plenty of other tension is around, stoking tensions in Kosovo through an assassination attempt adds to a generally combustible atmosphere and is very unwelcome," a senior Western diplomat said.

"This reinforces our case for the Socialists to stop wasting time and accept a solution to the election crisis according to the recommendations of OSCE investigators who called for opposition victories to be restored."
Serbia's Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition is campaigning to reverse Socialist authorities' annulment of election results in 14 major Serbian towns on grounds of murky "irregularities".

An opposition takeover at municipal level would start democratic reform in Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia, under communist/socialist rule since World War Two, by breaking leftist strangleholds on the main media and judiciary.

Multi-party electoral commissions declared a week ago that Zajedno had indeed won in Belgrade and Serbia's second city Nis. A Socialist appeal in Nis was rejected by its municipal court and Zajedno is preparing to take power there next week.

But cautious hopes of a breakthrough covering all 14 towns at issue were blunted on Monday when Belgrade's municipal court suspended the commission ruling there and asked the Supreme Court to decide the volatile matter.
Hours later, the high court ruled the Socialists had won a majority in the town of Sabac, ignoring contrary conclusions by international factfinders in another setback for Zajedno.

Informed political sources said on Tuesday the Socialists were considering getting the pliant Supreme Court to uphold their appeal in Belgrade, imposing provisional administration for two months and then holding new elections.

It was not clear whether this strategy might be expanded to cover other contested cities. But both diplomats and dissenters within Milosevic's leftist coalition, whose unity has frayed during the crisis, said Zajedno was certain to reject the move.

"I'm very doubtful whether the protest rallies would indeed stop, because provisional rule wouldn't solve anything with finality," said a source within the ruling bloc, comprised of socialists, neo-communists and left-wing moderates.
"I don't think Zajedno would accept the elimination of its campaign with all their domestic and foreign support. Why shouldn't they go for the whole pie within the OSCE framework?"

Zajedno, which planned to have taxi drivers blockade Belgrade bridges on Tuesday in their latest protest tactic, says it would boycott new elections and vows to keep agitating until the SPS explicitly admit defeat in all 14 towns.

Under current law, provisional government can be declared in a town if its assembly has not been convened within 60 days of an election -- the case in Belgrade. But new elections should be called two months later.
